title: Invest 92L Is Organizing in the Gulf. Check the Roof While It Is Dry.
description: As of Oct. 6, Invest 92L has a 90% chance of forming in the Gulf. Louisiana should watch it. Houston should photograph the roof before Friday.
html:
As of Tuesday morning, October 6, the National Hurricane Center is watching a broad low in the southwestern Gulf, tagged Invest 92L. A tropical depression is expected within about a day. The chance of formation is 90% over the next two days and 90% over the next week. If it becomes a tropical storm, the next name on the list is Isaias. There is no finished forecast cone yet, because it is not a named storm.

The center is expected to drift east, then turn north or northeast toward the northern Gulf Coast by the end of the week. The Hurricane Center told interests from Louisiana through the Florida Panhandle to pay attention. It did not put the upper Texas coast in that sentence. Houston-area forecasters at KPRC read the same pattern: a cold front should steer the core east of Southeast Texas. They have about a 20% chance of rain here Friday through Sunday, from outer bands, and they expect the heavy rain to stay east. Guidance they cited shows on the order of 5 to 9.5 inches from Louisiana into Florida. That number is not an official Hurricane Center total. It can change.

Why the roof still gets a look

A miss is not a promise. The track can shift before a cone exists, and a band on the west side of a Gulf storm is enough to find an old leak. The useful hour is today and tomorrow, while the shingles are dry. Do it from the yard.

  • Photograph each slope, the valleys, and the gutters. You want a before picture if Saturday brings a stain.
  • Clear leaves from gutters, downspouts, and valleys so water has somewhere to go.
  • Note any ceiling mark that is already there. Do not blame this weekend for a spot from September.
  • On tile or slate, stay off the roof. From the ground, look for a slipped tile, a cracked slate, or an open hip. Those do not fail the way a missing shingle tab does.
  • On a low-slope or flat roof, clear the drains and scuppers. An inch of rain in an hour ponds where a leaf mat is sitting.

The usual first leaks are the sidewall kickout, the chimney, and any spot that already holds water. The three spots that leak first is a short list if you want to know what you are looking at. Ponding on a low-slope roof is the commercial version of the same problem.

If water gets in

Bucket the drip. Leave the ladder alone while the roof is wet. A tarp is for an open hole, not for a slope that only looks tired. Nails across a whole field make the next repair worse. How that should be done is in tarping a roof after a Texas storm. If water is coming into the house around Houston, call the storm emergency line. Do not sign a contract with someone who arrived because the radar turned red. Core Four works Greater Houston from the Tomball shop. We are not a crew driving into Louisiana behind the storm.

If you are in Louisiana or the Panhandle, the heavier rain is the hazard on your side of the forecast. Clear the drains today. If the ceiling is already wet, that is a repair, not a project for after the weekend. The same photos help whoever you hire there.

Check the Hurricane Center again Wednesday. Recon is scheduled, and that is when a cone, if there is one, starts to mean something. Until then, the dry-day work is the part you control. The Houston homeowner storm checklist is the photo list. When you want someone on the roof after the weather, ask for an inspection or call (281) 541-0027.
